title: Stage 5: Querying
summary: Let clients filter, search and page through the task list with query string parameters and LINQ.

steps.title: Query strings
body: A real task list grows. Nobody wants all 5,000 tasks when they are looking for the open ones about shipping. This stage lets the client **filter**, **search** and **page** through the collection.
Those options travel in the **query string**: the part of the URL after `?`, written as `name=value` pairs joined by `&`.
- The **query string** adjusts how you want to see it: filtered, sorted, a page at a time.
- The **body** carries content you are sending, and a `GET` has none.
`/tasks?done=false` is still the tasks collection, seen through a filter. So the response is still a JSON array, and when nothing matches it is `200 OK` with `[]`, not a 404.
A handler parameter of a simple type (`int`, `bool`, `string`...) that is *not* named in the route is read from the query string:
Make them **nullable**. That is what marks them optional. A plain `bool pinned` would be required, and a request without it would be rejected with 400.

steps.prompt: Where does each piece of information belong in a request?
items: The id of the task to delete
Show only tasks that are done
The title of a new task
Which page of results to return
The id of the task to read
steps.explain: Identity goes in the route, options for viewing a collection go in the query string, and content goes in the body.

steps.prompt: A client sends `GET /notes` with no query string at all. What does the handler receive?
options: Nothing: the framework answers `400 Bad Request`
Nothing: the framework answers `404 Not Found`
steps.explain: A nullable parameter that is missing from the query string arrives as `null`, which lets you tell *not asked for* apart from *asked for false*. That difference matters: `?done=false` is a filter, and no `done` at all means no filter.

steps.title: Filtering with LINQ
body: Each filter is optional, so build the query up one step at a time. Start with everything, and narrow it only for the parameters that were sent:
Declaring `query` as `IEnumerable<Note>` matters: `Where` returns an `IEnumerable<Note>`, which cannot be assigned back to a variable typed as `List<Note>`.
Two filters combine naturally. Each `Where` narrows what the one before left, so `?pinned=true&search=milk` means *both* must hold.
People type search text in any case. Plain `Contains("ship")` is case-sensitive and would miss `Ship it`. Passing `StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase` fixes that.

code: var titles = new List<string> { "Learn C#", "Build an API", "Ship it" };
steps.explain: Without a comparison argument `Contains` is case-sensitive, so `SHIP` matches nothing. Ignoring case it finds `Ship it`. The letter `i` appears in `Build an API` and `Ship it`, and not in `Learn C#`.

steps.title: Filter and search
prompt: Extend `GET /tasks` with two optional query parameters.
| `done=true` or `done=false` | only tasks whose done state matches |
| `search=text` | only tasks whose title contains the text, ignoring case |
- With no query string, `GET /tasks` returns every task, as before.
- When both parameters are given, a task must pass both.
- No matches is `200 OK` with an empty array `[]`.
- The response is always a JSON array, in id order.

await Dojo.TryAsync("The earlier endpoints could be checked", async () =>
Dojo.Eq("GET /health still returns ok", "ok", await DojoWeb.Text(await http.GetAsync("/health")));

await Dojo.TryAsync("The done filter could be checked", async () =>
var r = await http.GetAsync("/tasks?done=true");
DojoWeb.Status("GET /tasks?done=true responds 200 OK", 200, r);
Dojo.Eq("GET /tasks?done=true returns only task 1", "1", Ids(await DojoWeb.Json(r)));
Dojo.Eq("GET /tasks?done=false returns tasks 2 and 3", "2,3", await IdsOf(http, "/tasks?done=false"));
await Dojo.TryAsync("The search filter could be checked", async () =>
Dojo.Eq("GET /tasks?search=API returns task 2 (\"Build an API\")", "2", await IdsOf(http, "/tasks?search=API"));
Dojo.Eq("GET /tasks?search=ship ignores case and returns task 3 (\"Ship it\")", "3", await IdsOf(http, "/tasks?search=ship"));
Dojo.Eq("GET /tasks?search=i matches inside words: tasks 2 and 3", "2,3", await IdsOf(http, "/tasks?search=i"));
var none = await http.GetAsync("/tasks?search=zzz");
DojoWeb.Status("GET /tasks?search=zzz responds 200 OK, not 404", 200, none);
Dojo.Eq("GET /tasks?search=zzz returns an empty array", "", Ids(await DojoWeb.Json(none)));
await Dojo.TryAsync("Combined filters could be checked", async () =>
Dojo.Eq("GET /tasks?done=false&search=build returns task 2", "2", await IdsOf(http, "/tasks?done=false&search=build"));
Dojo.Eq("GET /tasks?done=true&search=build returns nothing", "", await IdsOf(http, "/tasks?done=true&search=build"));
Dojo.Eq("the order of the parameters does not matter: ?search=build&done=false", "2", await IdsOf(http, "/tasks?search=build&done=false"));
var created = await http.PostAsJsonAsync("/tasks", new { title = "Document the API" });
DojoWeb.Status("POST /tasks still responds 201 Created", 201, created);
Dojo.Eq("a task created later is found too: ?search=api returns 2 and 4", "2,4", await IdsOf(http, "/tasks?search=api"));
await Patch(http, "/tasks/4/done", new { done = true });
Dojo.Eq("after ticking task 4 off, ?done=true returns 1 and 4", "1,4", await IdsOf(http, "/tasks?done=true"));
// "1,2,3" for a JSON array of tasks, so one row can check which tasks came back and in what order.
static string Ids(JsonElement json) => json.ValueKind == JsonValueKind.Array
? string.Join(",", json.EnumerateArray().Select(e => DojoWeb.Prop(e, "id")))
: "(not a JSON array)";
static JsonElement At(JsonElement json, int index) =>
json.ValueKind == JsonValueKind.Array && index < json.GetArrayLength() ? json[index] : default;
static async Task<string> IdsOf(HttpClient http, string url) => Ids(await DojoWeb.Json(await http.GetAsync(url)));
static bool HasError(JsonElement json) => !string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(DojoWeb.Prop(json, "error"));
static Task<HttpResponseMessage> Patch(HttpClient http, string url, object body) =>
http.PatchAsync(url, JsonContent.Create(body));
hints: Change the lambda from `() => tasks` to `(bool? done, string? search) => { ... }`. Both are nullable so that both are optional.
Start with `IEnumerable<TaskItem> query = tasks;` and add a `Where` only when the parameter is not null: `if (done is not null) query = query.Where(t => t.Done == done);`
For the search: `query = query.Where(t => t.Title.Contains(search, StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase));` and finish with `return query.ToList();`

steps.title: Paging
body: A filter narrows the list, but the result can still be huge. **Paging** hands it out in slices: *page 3, with 20 per page*.
Two LINQ methods do the slicing:
Page 1 skips nothing. Page 3 with a page size of 20 skips 40 and takes the next 20. `Take` is happy to return fewer when the list runs out, and a page beyond the end is simply empty.
Paging needs a **fixed order**. If the order could change between two requests, a client walking through the pages would see some items twice and miss others. Sorting by id makes the order explicit.
The client controls `page` and `pageSize`, so treat them as input to be checked:
- A **maximum** page size. Without one, `?pageSize=10000000` asks your server for everything in one response.
- **Minimums**, because `page=0` or `pageSize=-5` would hand `Skip` and `Take` nonsense.
`Math.Clamp(value, min, max)` forces a number into a range:
Quietly correcting an out-of-range value is one reasonable policy. Rejecting it with 400 is another. Whichever you pick, document it and apply it everywhere.

steps.explain: Page 3 skips two full pages (4 items) and takes the next 2. Page 4 skips 6 and asks for 2, but only one item is left, so `Take` returns just that one.

steps.prompt: A client asked for 500 per page. Complete the line so the size falls back to 10 when missing and always stays between 1 and 50. The program should print `50`.
steps.explain: `pageSize ?? 10` supplies the default, and `Math.Clamp(value, 1, 50)` pulls anything below 1 up to 1 and anything above 50 down to 50.

steps.prompt: There are 3 tasks. A client requests `GET /tasks?page=9&pageSize=2`. What is the best response?
options: `400 Bad Request` with an error message
`200 OK` with the last page that does exist
steps.explain: The collection `/tasks` exists, and the request is well formed. This slice of it happens to be empty. An empty array is also what tells a client that pages through the list that it has reached the end.

steps.title: Page through the results
prompt: Add paging to `GET /tasks` with two more optional query parameters.
| `page` | `1` | 1 and up. Anything lower counts as 1. |
| `pageSize` | `10` | 1 to 50. Lower counts as 1, higher counts as 50. |
- Tasks come back in id order.
- Filter first, then page: `?done=false&page=2&pageSize=1` is the *second open task*.
- A page past the end is `200 OK` with `[]`.
- With no query string, `GET /tasks` now returns the first 10 tasks. With the three starting tasks that is still all of them.
The `done` and `search` filters must keep working, alone and together with paging.
